stem: According to the Homestead Act, what did a settler have to do before receiving title to the land?

stimulus.source_note: Homestead Act of 1862, 12 Stat. 392. Public domain. Text verified against the National Park Service transcription (home.nps.gov/home/homestead-act-of-1862.htm) and Wikisource (en.wikisource.org/wiki/Homestead_Act).
stimulus.text:
Homestead Act of 1862, Sections 1-2 (ellipses mark omissions):

"That any person who is the head of a family, or who has arrived at the age of twenty-one years, and is a citizen of the United States, or who shall have filed his declaration of intention to become such, ... shall ... be entitled to enter one quarter section or a less quantity of unappropriated public lands ... Provided, That any person owning and residing on land may ... enter other land lying contiguous to his or her said land, which shall not, with the land so already owned and occupied, exceed in the aggregate one hundred and sixty acres."

"And upon filing the said affidavit with the register or receiver, and on payment of ten dollars, he or she shall thereupon be permitted to enter the quantity of land specified: Provided, however, That no certificate shall be given or patent issued therefor until the expiration of five years from the date of such entry."

options.text: Pay the full market price of the land to the federal government
options.misconception: Background: the act charged only a ten-dollar filing fee; the land itself was free to qualifying settlers.

options.text: Live on and farm the land for five years, after paying a ten-dollar fee
Serve two years in the United States Army on the frontier
options.misconception: Background: military service was one way to qualify, but the act did not require it of every settler.

options.text: Sell half of the first harvest to the government at a fixed price
options.misconception: Background: the act said nothing about selling crops to the government; its conditions were residence and cultivation.

rationales.A: Background: the act gave the land away. The only payment named is the ten-dollar filing fee, not a purchase price.
rationales.B: Section 2 names the bargain plainly: a ten-dollar fee to enter the claim, then five years of residence and cultivation before the patent issues.
rationales.C: Background: army or navy service could substitute for the age requirement, but it was an alternative way to qualify, not a condition of title.
rationales.D: Background: no harvest sale appears anywhere in the act. Title turned on living on the land and farming it for five years.
rationales.general:
Picture a settler at the land office, ten dollars in hand and five hard years ahead.
1. Read what the act asks for: a fee, an affidavit, and five years of residence and cultivation.
2. Rule out the prices and duties the act never names. No purchase price, no army term, no harvest sale.
3. Name the deal. Free land in exchange for five years of living on it and farming it.
Remember: a homestead was earned by living on the land, not bought with cash.
